claims.text: A thin, conformal HfO2 coating applied by ALD will improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding.
HfO2-coated zirconium-alloy cladding will retain suitability for reactor service.
The proposed intervention is deposition of an approximately 50 nm HfO2 coating using ALD.
Exposure at approximately 1200°C for about one hour is representative of a high-temperature accident transient.
ALD will produce a continuous, nanocrystalline HfO2 layer on the cladding.
The continuous HfO2 layer will act as an oxygen-diffusion barrier.
The HfO2 coating forms a thermodynamically stable, dense microstructure under the stated conditions.
The HfO2 microstructure slows inward oxygen diffusion.
Slower inward oxygen diffusion reduces zirconium oxidation kinetics and rapid zirconium-oxide formation.
Limiting rapid zirconium oxidation reduces attendant exothermic reactions during high-temperature exposure.
The HfO2 coating remains chemically compatible with zirconium-alloy cladding under normal service conditions.
At approximately 1200°C for approximately one hour, coated cladding will show about 50% lower oxidation weight gain than uncoated cladding.
At approximately 1200°C for approximately one hour, coated cladding will develop a thinner oxide layer than uncoated cladding.
The expected improvement is limited to high-temperature transient oxidation and may not extend to long-term aging or other temperature regimes.
The coating may affect cladding thermal conductivity and neutron economy.
The long-term durability of the HfO2 layer under irradiation and thermal cycling is uncertain.
Potential interactions between HfO2 and the zirconium alloy at the coating interface are uncertain.
